spoken: In November 1942, Allied commanders hoped to take Tunis within weeks.
It took six months, and the fighting crossed Tunisia, from its southern desert to its northern hills.
Soldiers came from five continents, and they fought among the towns, farms and villages of the Tunisians.
This is the story of the Tunisian campaign, from November 1942 to May 1943.
In 1942, Tunisia was a French protectorate. Moncef Bey reigned, but a French resident-general held the real power.
He was Admiral Jean-Pierre Esteva, appointed by Vichy France, which had signed an armistice with Germany in 1940.
On the 8th of November, in Operation Torch, about 125,000 American and British soldiers, sailors and airmen landed in Morocco and Algeria.
Within three days, the French there stopped fighting. The real prize lay east, in Tunisia, facing Sicily.
Germany moved faster. From the 9th of November, German planes landed at El Aweena, by Tunis, and Esteva did not stop them.
By mid-November, about 15,000 German and 9,000 Italian troops held Tunis and Bizerte.
But General Georges Barray's French troops turned against the Germans, and fought them at Medjez el Bab on the 19th of November.
From Algiers, over 600 kilometres away, the British First Army raced east, with American tanks and French troops.
On the 28th of November, they reached Djedeida, just 21 kilometres from Tunis, and got no closer.
Axis fighters flew from hard runways by Tunis, Allied planes from distant dirt fields that the winter rain turned to mud.
Counter-attacks drove the Allies back to Medjez el Bab, and on the 24th of December, General Eisenhower called a halt.
All winter, the front ran along the mountain ridges. The British held the north, the French the centre, and the Americans the south.
In January, German attacks fell on the French in the centre. Poorly equipped, they resisted hard, but were overrun.
French army records count some 73,000 French troops in Tunisia by March, about 50,000 of them North Africans.
Tunisian riflemen fought among them, with makeshift equipment, beside the Americans and the British.
From the east came Britain's Eighth Army, which had driven the Axis armies out of Egypt and across Libya.
With it came New Zealanders, Indians, Free French soldiers from Chad and Greeks, and airmen from Australia and South Africa.
Facing them were Germans and Italians. The Fifth Panzer Army held the north, and the Italian First Army the south.
In February, the Axis struck the Americans in the south. It was the American army's first campaign against the German army.
On the 14th of February, panzers struck at Sidi Bou Zid, where American infantry sat on hills too far apart to help each other.
In two days, the American First Armored Division lost 98 tanks and about half its strength, by the historian Martin Blumenson's count.
The Allies fell back about 80 kilometres, to the passes of the western ridge.
On the 19th and 20th of February, German and Italian troops under Erwin Rommel broke through the Kasserine Pass.
They were held at Sbiba, Jebel el Hamra and Tahla, where massed British and American guns stopped them, on the 22nd of February.
The National World War Two Museum names the causes. Commanders had not seen the ground, divisions were split up, coordination was poor, and the troops were new.
Then the Allies changed. Harold Alexander took command of their armies, and George S. Patton of the American Two Corps, on the 6th of March.
On the 23rd of March, at El Guettar, American troops held against a panzer division.
In the south, the Italian First Army under General Giovanni Messeh, with German divisions, held the Mareth Line.
France had built it in the 1930s against an attack from Italian Libya. Now it faced the British, coming from Libya.
On the 6th of March, at Medenine, Rommel attacked and lost between 44 and 56 tanks, by the British count. Three days later, he left Africa.
On the night of the 20th of March, Montgomery's frontal attack across the Wadi Zigzow, near the village of Zarat, was thrown back.
Meanwhile the New Zealand Corps, with General Luh-clair's Free French, went some 200 kilometres round the hills, to the Tebaga Gap.
This left hook became Montgomery's main attack. On the 26th of March, at four in the afternoon, with the sun behind it, it broke through.
The British official history judged that the hook won the battle, but could not make a victory of it. The Axis army got away.
The Axis stood next at the Wadi Akarit, north of Gahbess, in a gap between the sea and salt marshes.
On the night of the 5th of April, Indian and Gurkha soldiers climbed its hills in silence, with Scottish and English divisions beside them.
Italian and German troops resisted hard, but that night they withdrew. On the 7th of April, the Eighth Army met the Americans.
It pushed north through Sfax and Sousse, more than 200 kilometres, and the two Allied fronts became one.
On the 19th and 20th of April, the Eighth Army took Enfidaville and the rock village of Takroona, from Italian and German defenders.
In the west, the British took Longstop Hill and the Americans Hill six-oh-nine, by the 1st of May, at a heavy cost on both sides.
On the 6th of May, the First Army broke through west of Tunis, with Indian infantry and tanks brought from the Eighth Army.
On the 7th of May, British tanks entered Tunis, and American infantry entered Bizerte.
The Axis armies were cut in two. British tanks sealed off Cap Bon, and French troops closed in round Zaghouan.
Behind them lay the sea, watched day and night by Allied ships and aircraft. Only a few hundred men escaped.
On the 13th of May 1943, the Italian Marshal Giovanni Messeh surrendered the last Axis army in Africa.
How many prisoners were taken? The British official history counts 238,243, and the American army's official historian about 275,000.
Historians usually say about a quarter of a million. In Germany, the defeat was compared with Stalingrad.
The Allies lost between 70,000 and 76,000 men, killed, wounded or missing, by American and British counts, and more than 11,000 of them were killed.
German and Italian losses are less certain. The historian Rick Atkinson estimates about 8,500 German and 3,700 Italian dead.
And the Tunisians? The historian Mark Willis writes that civilians, caught between the two sides, suffered tremendous losses.
Almost all of Tunisia's major cities and towns were destroyed or badly damaged, and its economy was wrecked.
Under the occupation, the Germans had forced about 5,000 Jewish men in Tunisia into labour camps, many near the front.
The end of the fighting did not free Tunisia. On the 14th of May, the French deposed Moncef Bey, accusing him of collaboration.
For the Allies, it was a beginning. On the 10th of July 1943, they landed in Sicily, some sailing from Tunisia, and soon Mussolini fell.
The American army drew lessons. It learned to keep units close enough to help each other, to keep its tanks together, and to make infantry, tanks, guns and planes work as one.
It left Tunisia with thousands of seasoned soldiers, and commanders such as Patton and Bradley led them in Sicily.
Six months of war crossed Tunisia. Remember the soldiers of every army, and the Tunisians whose country it was.
